extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, criminalists, and forensic/clinical psychologists who assess witness reliability
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the credibility, accuracy, and limitations of witnesses (children, the elderly, and adults) by examining sensory capacity, memory, attitude, conception differences, and contextual influences on perception and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child sensory development and acuity
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses of children are especially keen and properly developed. It is anatomically true that very young children do not hear well; ... Their sense of smell ... very dull, and develops at the time of puberty (though observers differ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the child's sensory capacities relative to age: hearing, smell, vision may be immature or developing. Use age-appropriate expectations when judging perceptual testimony and consider rebutting or qualifying claims that depend on a sense not yet fully developed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child accuracy of representation / subjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Children tell untruths without lying. They say only what they have in mind, but they do not know and care very little whether their mental content is objective and exists outside of them, or whether only half real and the rest fanciful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between deliberate deception and subjective/fanciful reporting. Look for the identifiable 'subjective half' of the child's story (which legal experience can often separate from fact). Do not equate a child's fantasy or mistaken belief with intentional falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child lacunae in comprehension and reconstructive errors
rubrics_metrics.description: There are lacunae in the child’s comprehension of what it perceives. When it observes an event, it may completely understand the first part, find the second part altogether new and unintelligible, ... If the child is only half-interested, it will try to fill out these lacunae by reflection and synthesis, and may conceivably make serious blunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe for gaps in the child’s understanding and beware of post-hoc filling-in. Question about sequence and parts separately; check for inconsistencies that indicate synthesis rather than direct perception, especially for events further back in time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child early-memory capacity but limited descriptive range
rubrics_metrics.description: Very small children can recall experiences at thirty-two, twenty-four, and even eighteen months, and told them correctly. ... their circle of ideas being so small that the commonest experiences are excluded from adequate description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that very young children may retain factual memories from early life, but their ability to describe commonplace details is limited by vocabulary and conceptual range. Use focused, simple factual questions (Who? Where? Was anyone there?) to elicit useful information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child unreliability of time determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Children’s determinations of time are unreliable. Yesterday and to-day are easily confused by small children, and a considerably advanced intelligence is necessary to distinguish between yesterday and a week ago, or even a week and a month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on children for accurate dating of events without external anchors. Use concrete reference points (meals, holidays, school days) rather than abstract calendar intervals when establishing timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit of question to child's concepts / individualization
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions of the child’s bringing-up, the things he learned to know, are what we must first of all learn. If the question in hand can fit into the notion the child possesses, he will answer better ... than if a very clever child who is foreign to the notions of the defined situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor questions to the child's lived experience and vocabulary. Determine whether the child has the relevant concepts; if not, reframe or provide contextual cues. Collect background on upbringing and learned concepts to interpret answers properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicality more important than raw intelligence (children)
rubrics_metrics.description: I should take intelligence only to be of next importance ... advise giving up separating clever from stupid children in favor of separating practical and unpractical children. For the rôle of witness the child’s practicality is the important thing. The practical child will see, observe, properly understand, and reproduce a group of things that the unpractical child has not even observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a child's practical engagement with the world (observational habits, common-sense recall) rather than formal intelligence tests when judging likely reliability of testimony. A less 'clever' but practical child can be a superior witness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child imitation and diminished responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The child does many things simply as blind imitation. ... if a child is imitating an imitable person, a parent, a teacher, etc., its responsibility is at an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a child's alleged wrongdoing or testimony echoes an adult model, consider imitation as an explanation and evaluate culpability/credibility accordingly. Ascertain who the child was exposed to and whether the act was imitative rather than volitional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralization from juvenile delinquency anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: When this literature is tested the conclusion is inevitable that there has been overbold generalization. ... Individual and noisy cases require so much attention that their character is assigned to the whole class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from sensational or noisy juvenile cases to all children. Treat exceptional or striking incidents as potentially unrepresentative; seek population-level or corroborative evidence before drawing broad inferences about children’s tendencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Child moral comprehension differs from adult legal/moral categories
rubrics_metrics.description: The child knows very well that stealing is dishonorable, sinful, criminal. But it does not know that counterfeiting, treachery, and arson are forbidden. ... It is just as difficult for the child to become subjective. The child is more of an egoist than the adult ... it does not discover the limits between what is permissible, and what is not permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the child understands the specific legal or moral distinction at issue. Do not assume knowledge of nuanced legal concepts; clarify the child's moral framework and how it maps to the alleged wrongful act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senility: simplified, narrowed mental organization
rubrics_metrics.description: The mental organization of senility is essentially simplified and narrowed to a few types. Its activities are lessened, its influences and aims are compressed, the present brings little and is little remembered, so that its collective character is determined by a resultant, composed of those forces that have influenced the man’s past life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating elderly witnesses, expect cognitive simplification and narrowed concerns; consider how life-long dispositions may dominate present accounts. Use probing to separate durable past narratives from immediate factual recall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senile tendency to mix fact and judgment; embittered vs excusing types
rubrics_metrics.description: Senility presents fact and judgment together. ... Everything it tells is bound up with its judgment, and its judgment is either negative or positive. ... Accurate observation will reveal only two types of senility. There is the embittered type, and there is the character expressed in the phrase, 'to understand all is to forgive all.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether an elderly witness’s account is colored by embitterment or excusing benevolence. Expect that facts are presented together with evaluative comments; attempt to disentangle factual report from lifelong judgment coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senile bias toward remote memories over recent events
rubrics_metrics.description: The familiar fact that very old men remember things long past better than immediate occurrences, is to be explained by ... the ancient brain retains only that which it has frequently experienced. Old experiences are recalled ... while the new ... had not time to find a place before being forgotten.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat detailed remote recollections from elderly witnesses as more accessible but not necessarily more relevant; recent events may be under-reported or confounded with remote memories. Cross-check recent-event claims with contemporaneous evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal equation (differences in perceptual timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomers ... showed that various observers of contemporaneous events do not observe at the same time. This fact is called 'the personal equation.' ... events which succeed each other very rapidly may cause individual observers to have quite different images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for inter-observer timing differences when reconciling rapid events; accept that simultaneous witnesses can perceive and report different sequences. Use synchronized external evidence where possible (timestamps, video).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in observation / selective attention and parsing ability
rubrics_metrics.description: The observer is not he who sees the thing, but who sees of what parts it is made. ... One man overlooks half because he is inattentive or is looking at the wrong place; another substitutes his own inferences for objects, while another tends to observe the quality of objects, and neglects their quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate what each witness habitually attends to (parts vs whole, quality vs quantity) and test for attentional blind spots. Distinguish failure to perceive from failure to recall; elicit details about vantage point and focus of attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude / feeling (stimmung) shapes perception and report
rubrics_metrics.description: Attitude or feeling—this indefinable factor exercises a great influence on conception and interpretation. ... a minute influence (weather, a cigar, a peal of bells) may create or alter our attitudes for a long time ... I am convinced that if I had been called to testify in my sad state, I would have told the story otherwise than normally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probe witness mood/attitude at time of perception and at time of testimony; consider how temporary emotional states hospitalize perception and can skew descriptions. Ask about intervening events (loss, fatigue, recent stressors) that could explain atypical tone or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indifference and neurotic detachment reduce reporting accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: There is ... a not rare and complete indifference to feeling, and in consciousness an essential lack of feeling-tone in perception. ... This condition is very dangerous in the law court, because ... a person utterly detached ... does not tell the judge of his condition, probably because he does not know anything about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to witnesses who are indifferent or detached; they may provide shadowy, superficial accounts and fail to report their own condition. Specifically ask about health, mood, and states of mind at the time to reveal otherwise-unreported detachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bodily conditions and physical position affect judgment and memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily conditions are still more remarkable in effecting differences in point of view. ... this attitude varies with the difference in the quantity of blood in the brain in these two positions ... We might like an idea when lying down that displeases us when we stand up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the witness’s physical state (tiredness, illness, recumbent vs upright) both at the time of the event and during recollection. Physical state can alter judgment, decision-making, and the content of recollection—ask about posture, sleep, and recent exertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-event reflection and rumination can alter memory
rubrics_metrics.description: When a witness ... reflects about some event while he is in bed. When he thinks of it again he is convinced ... that the matter really occurred in quite another way than he had newly supposed it to. ... he sticks to his first story, although that might have been incorrect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between contemporaneous recollection and memories formed/altered by rumination. Ask whether the witness has thought about the event since it occurred and whether they discussed it with others; treat initial contemporaneous statements as having special evidentiary value when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition and convenience of comparison affect accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Two lines of unequal length seem equal when they diverge, although their difference is recognized immediately if they are parallel, close together, and start from the same level. ... Juxtaposition is frequently important ... only if he has [discovered the right juxtaposition], can his comparison have been good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a witness had opportunity to compare relevant items side-by-side. When comparisons are required (sizes, distances, quantities), note whether conditions allowed valid juxtaposition; lack of it undermines reliability of comparative judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest and focus determine what a witness observes
rubrics_metrics.description: Conception and interpretation are considerably dependent on the interest which is brought to the object examined. ... The child was interested only in the chocolate, and hence, understood it and its nearest environment—the hand and the sleeve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the witness’s interests and subjective focus at the time of the event: what attracted attention and what was ignored. Corroborate claims about peripheral aspects the witness was unlikely to notice given their interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semantic variability and dangers of ambiguous/foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: Words have become symbols of concepts, and simple words have come to mean involved mathematical and philosophical ideas. ... The use of foreign words, in a sense different from that used by us, may lead us far astray. Taine: 'Love and amour, girl and jeune fille, song and chanson, are not identical although they are substituted for one another.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify meanings of key words used by witnesses—especially culturally specific or foreign-language terms. Avoid assuming uniform definitions; when testimony hinges on terminology, unpack the witness’s intended meaning and consider linguistic/cultural misunderstandings as a source of conflict.
